source.title: Open-Weight LLM Fine-Tuning Defenses are Susceptible to Simple Attacks
source.authors: Kevin Kuo; Chhavi Yadav; Virginia Smith

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some tables are flattened, but the results used here can be assigned from their layout.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests direction-based refusal removal and its effect on harmful outputs, including a weight-edit version of abliteration. It uses a different procedure from the claim’s all-layer, all-position activation projection: it edits weights and searches over one layer at a time.
record.gate_note: The study reports harmful-output attack success rates for abliteration and abliteration combined with prefilling, capability measurements after abliteration, and a representation analysis. Prefill-only results do not test the direction-based claims and are not rows. The text also mentions prior-work results, which are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study applies a difference-in-means refusal-direction ablation as a single-layer weight edit, searched over layers and scaling factors. It measures harmful-output ASR on Base, SEAM and TAR Llama models, plus capability after ablation. It also trains against ablation (ART) and measures the robustness gained. The method differs from the original's all-layer activation ablation, and the setting (fine-tuning-safeguarded checkpoints) is new.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. Abliteration and prefilling raise ASR on TAR/SEAM-safeguarded models from under 10% to 16–97% without fine-tuning. ART cuts ASR by about 10–20 points and composes with TAR, but no defense closes the gap. Robust safety needs defenses that remove harmful knowledge rather than refusal-only safeguards.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a harmful-minus-benign difference in residual-stream activations and projects the direction out, but implements this as a weight edit on one layer at a time, searches layers and scaling factors, and uses only the last prompt token to compute the direction rather than ablating every layer and position together.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack success varies with safeguard, model size, benchmark, selected layer and scaling factor, and attack budget. The paper says abliteration is sensitive to layer choice; it reports best-of-N results and lower-budget alternatives. Prefilling’s effect also varies by model and safeguard, but prefilling-only results are not cataloged as direction-based findings.

fits_no_version.finding: PCA shows abliterated harmful prompts that shift toward harmless representations are often jailbroken, and TAR separates the classes most.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safeguard strength tracks post-ablation separation of harmful and harmless representations.

record.problems: The main abliteration results use best-of-N layer and scaling-factor search and the authors note that such a search may overstate a single attack’s strength. Abliteration directions use 128 harmful and 128 benign prompts, and only the last prompt token is used. Attack success is judged by a 13B Llama-2-chat HarmBench judge in the main evaluation. No uncertainty intervals or significance tests are reported. Capability evidence after abliteration is limited to the reported Alpaca and MMLU measures.
record.rows_left_out: The six-row limit was not reached. Prefill-only results are omitted because they do not test direction removal. Other reported results not cataloged include Table 2’s 8B rows, additional budgets in Table 3, the full model-family ablation in Table 10, Table 4’s safeguard utility results without abliteration, and ART capability and fine-tuning evaluations in Tables 7–8; these were omitted to prioritize the direct direction-removal results, capability check after abliteration, and ART’s abliteration results.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to induce refusal; simultaneous all-layer, all-position activation ablation.
Whether prompt jailbreaks or prefilling work by suppressing the direction.
Effectively all; only an observational PCA is reported.
Safeguard training (SEAM vs TAR) changes abliteration effectiveness, but whether one removable direction exists is not tested directly.

missing.what: Gemma3-1B-IT abliteration ASR without ART (Base 93, SEAM 80, TAR 76), and Abliterate+Prefill with and without ART
Abliteration ASR on Llama3.1-8B across RepNoise, Vaccine, Booster, ART, TAR+ART: ART 99→65, TAR+ART 67
Qwen and Gemma 1–2B abliteration ASR (e.g. Qwen SEAM 1→16, Gemma Base 6→93)

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. Best-of-N per-prompt success over all layers inflates ASR, as the authors acknowledge. The paper is internally inconsistent: the Table 3/9 'Full' TAR values (AdvBench 68, HarmBench 77) conflict with Table 1 (62, 33). Table 8 uses a different judge (BeaverDam-7B). The control rows can stay as baselines.

versions.untested_parts: It does not add the direction to induce refusals on harmless requests. Abliteration is applied to one layer at a time, not simultaneously at every layer and position. Capability retention is evaluated only on the reported Alpaca and MMLU measures and settings.
Tests the authors’ weight-edit implementation on the study’s checkpoints, not a broad sample of released models or independent third-party abliteration edits.

Tests abliteration itself and ART training against abliteration. It does not establish that other jailbreak attacks work by suppressing this direction, or test ART across a broad range of models and settings.
No direct test of an affine refusal set, a cone, or multiple refusal directions.
The representation analysis is observational and does not directly probe or causally establish separate harmfulness-judgment and refusal representations.
The study evaluates model families but computes directions for each model; it does not test transfer of a direction across languages, variants, or base-to-instruct models.
It compares models under different safeguards but does not test when or how refusal training determines whether a single removable direction exists.

rows.check: A PCA scatter of one abliterated model cannot show whether harmfulness and refusal are encoded separately. The authors instead hypothesize that harm discrimination drives refusal.
